summary: Describes version 3 of LDAP, a protocol for accessing directories based on the X.500 model without the heavy resource needs of the X.500 access protocol. It was replaced by RFCs 4510, 4511, 4512 and 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a lighter way to look things up in a big online directory of people and computers. Newer documents replaced it.

questions: what is a distinguished name in ldap
subtitle: A lightweight way to read and update X.500-style directories over a plain TCP connection.

tldr.problem: Directories built on the X.500 model were costly to use because the X.500 Directory Access Protocol (DAP) carries heavy resource requirements, which put them out of reach of simple management and browsing applications.
tldr.mechanism: LDAPv3 carries a compact set of operations (bind, search, modify, add, delete, modify DN, compare, abandon and extended) directly over TCP, with most data encoded as ordinary strings, and adds referrals, SASL authentication, UTF-8 text and extension points.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2251 was a Proposed Standard that is now replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4511, RFC 4512 and RFC 4513. The IESG note discouraged deploying update functionality until mandatory authentication was standardized.

today: RFC 2251 is a Proposed Standard that has been replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4511, RFC 4512 and RFC 4513. It was also updated by RFC 3377 and RFC 3771.

sections.title: Purpose and Key Changes in Version 3
sections.content:
LDAP provides access to directories that support the X.500 models without the resource requirements of the X.500 Directory Access Protocol (DAP). It targets management applications and browser applications that need read and write interactive access, and when used with an X.500 directory it is meant to complement DAP.

Version 3 supports all protocol elements of LDAPv2 (RFC 1777) and runs directly over TCP or another transport. It adds referrals to other servers, SASL mechanisms for authentication and other security services, internationalized names and values through the ISO 10646 character set, extension points for new operations and controls, and schema published in the directory for clients to read.

The model is simple: a client sends a request describing an operation and the server performs it and returns a response. Requests and responses need not be synchronous, and may be exchanged in any order as long as the client eventually gets a response for every request that needs one.

The IESG note warns that update operations needed secure authentication, but no mandatory mechanism was standardized. Implementors were discouraged from deploying update functionality until such a standard was published, while read-only use was encouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP lets a small program ask a big phone book for information without a lot of fuss. You send a question, and the phone book sends an answer back.

sections.title: The Directory Data Model
sections.content:
Servers jointly provide access to a Directory Information Tree (DIT) made of entries. An entry's name is its Distinguished Name (DN), formed by joining the relative distinguished names (RDNs) along the path from the root. An example is CN=Steve Kille, O=Isode Limited, C=GB. An RDN must be unique among its siblings.

An entry is a set of attributes, each with a type and one or more values. The type decides the value syntax and how values are matched. For example, mail values are IA5 (ASCII) strings compared without regard to case. Each entry must have an objectClass attribute, which together with the schema determines the attributes the entry may hold. Servers must not let clients add attributes the schema does not permit.

Operational attributes such as creatorsName, createTimestamp, modifiersName and modifyTimestamp are maintained by the server and are returned only when asked for by name.

Schema is published in subschema entries. A server that holds entries and lets clients modify them must provide these entries. Every server also exposes a root DSE, named by the zero-length DN, with attributes such as namingContexts, supportedLDAPVersion, supportedControl, supportedExtension, supportedSASLMechanisms and altServer.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a family tree where every person has a name tag, and each person also carries a card listing facts about them. The root card tells you what the whole phone book can do.

sections.title: Messages, Results and Encoding
sections.content:
Every operation travels inside one envelope, the LDAPMessage, which carries a messageID, the operation itself and optional controls. Responses repeat the message ID of their request. A client must not reuse a message ID that is still outstanding on the same connection, and the maximum value is 2147483647.

Text is ISO 10646 encoded as UTF-8. The protocol is described in ASN.1 and normally encoded with a restricted subset of the Basic Encoding Rules: only the definite length form, only primitive OCTET STRINGs, a true BOOLEAN encoded as hex FF, and default values left out. Clients and servers must ignore elements of a SEQUENCE whose tags they do not recognize.

Each result is an LDAPResult with a result code, a matched DN and an optional human-readable errorMessage. Apart from success, compareFalse and compareTrue, every code means the operation could not be completed in full. If a server cannot parse the envelope at all, it sends a notice of disconnection with protocolError and closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question and answer goes into a standard envelope with a number on it, so you can match each answer to the question it belongs to.

sections.title: The Operations
sections.content:
Bind authenticates the client. The client gives a protocol version, a name and either a simple cleartext password or a sasl mechanism with credentials. Some SASL mechanisms need several bind requests in a row. Unlike LDAPv2, a client need not bind first; an unbound client is treated as unauthenticated, and a failed rebind leaves the connection anonymous. Unbind ends the session and has no response.

Search takes a base object, a scope, an alias rule, a size limit, a time limit (in seconds), a typesOnly flag, a filter and a list of attributes. Filters combine and, or and not with equality, substring, greater-or-equal, less-or-equal, presence, approximate and extensible matches, and are evaluated with three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, Undefined). The server answers with zero or more entries, zero or more continuation references, and a final SearchResultDone.

The update operations are Modify (a list of add, delete and replace changes applied atomically in order), Add (the parent must exist and the entry must not), Delete (leaf entries only) and Modify DN (rename an entry or move a subtree). Compare tests one assertion against an entry, and Abandon asks the server to stop an outstanding operation and has no response.
sections.plainLanguage: You can show your ID, ask the phone book a question, add a new name, fix a name, cross one out, or ask it to stop looking. Some changes happen all at once or not at all.

sections.title: Referrals, Controls and Extended Operations
sections.content:
A server that does not hold the target entry can return a referral: one or more LDAP URLs of other servers, any of which can progress the operation. For a search that spans several naming contexts, the server instead returns continuation references, and the client must issue a new search for each one. Clients must not loop between servers, and those that count referrals must handle a DIT with at least ten layers of naming contexts.

A control adds information to a single request. It is identified by an object identifier and marked critical or not. If a server does not recognize a critical control, it must refuse to perform the operation; a non-critical one it does not recognize is ignored. This document defines no controls.

The extended operation lets other documents or private implementations define new request and response types, each with its own object identifier. A server that does not recognize the request name returns protocolError.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask the wrong librarian, they point you to the right one. Special notes on your question can say "you must do this exactly" or "do it if you can."

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
LDAP is meant for connection-oriented, reliable transports. Over TCP, the LDAPMessage PDUs map directly onto the byte stream. Servers may listen on the assigned port, 389, or on another port, and clients must be able to contact servers on any valid TCP port.

The protocol offers the LDAPv2-style simple authentication with a cleartext password, plus any SASL mechanism, which can also negotiate integrity and privacy services. Using a cleartext password where the transport cannot guarantee confidentiality is strongly discouraged. When SASL is used, the name field of the bind request is not protected against modification, so a DN agreed through the SASL credentials takes precedence.

Implementations that cache entries must keep access controls in place when serving more than one client.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling your password out loud in a crowded room is a bad idea. LDAP lets you use a secret handshake instead, or whisper in a private room.

items.label: operationsError
items.desc: Internal error, or a request refused because the client has not bound.

items.label: protocolError
items.desc: Unrecognized version number or incorrect PDU structure.

items.label: sizeLimitExceeded
items.desc: A search hit its size limit.

items.label: referral
items.desc: Contact another server to progress the operation.

items.label: noSuchObject
items.desc: The named entry was not found; the matched DN shows how far the name matched.

items.label: invalidCredentials
items.desc: Wrong password or unusable SASL credentials.

items.label: entryAlreadyExists
items.desc: An entry of that name already exists.
